# waterui-ffi

[](#waterui-ffi)

FFI bindings layer that bridges Rust view trees to native platform backends.

## Overview

[](#overview)

`waterui-ffi` is the C FFI layer at the heart of WaterUI's cross-platform architecture. It provides a type-safe, efficient bridge between Rust application logic and native UI backends, enabling WaterUI apps to render as true native widgets rather than custom-drawn pixels.

This crate serves three critical roles:

1.  **Entry Point Generation**: The `export!()` macro generates the C ABI entry points (`waterui_init`, `waterui_app`) that native backends call to initialize and run Rust applications.
    
2.  **Type Conversion**: Implements `IntoFFI` and `IntoRust` traits to safely convert between Rust types (views, reactive values, colors, fonts) and C-compatible representations that can cross the FFI boundary.
    
3.  **C Header Generation**: Uses `cbindgen` to automatically generate `waterui.h`, which is consumed by Swift (Apple backend) and Kotlin/JNI (Android backend) to understand the FFI contract.
    

The FFI layer is designed to work in `no_std` environments and minimizes unsafe code through carefully designed abstractions.

## Installation

[](#installation)

Add to your `Cargo.toml`:

\[dependencies\]
waterui = "0.2"
waterui-ffi = "0.1"

For applications, you typically only need the `export!()` macro - all other FFI details are handled internally by WaterUI.

## Quick Start

[](#quick-start)

Every WaterUI application uses the FFI layer to expose itself to native platforms:

use waterui::prelude::\*;
use waterui::app::App;

// Your application entry point
pub fn app(env: Environment) -> App {
    App::new(main, env)
}

fn main() -> impl View {
    text("Hello, WaterUI!")
}

// This macro generates waterui\_init() and waterui\_app() FFI entry points
waterui\_ffi::export!();

The `export!()` macro expands to:

#\[no\_mangle\]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn waterui\_init() -> \*mut WuiEnv {
    // Initialize runtime, logging, executors
    let env = waterui::Environment::new();
    env.into\_ffi()
}

#\[no\_mangle\]
pub unsafe extern "C" fn waterui\_app(env: \*mut WuiEnv) -> WuiApp {
    let env = env.into\_rust();
    let app = app(env);  // Call your app() function
    app.into\_ffi()
}

Native backends then call these functions to initialize and retrieve the root view tree.

## Core Concepts

[](#core-concepts)

### FFI Conversion Traits

[](#ffi-conversion-traits)

The crate defines two fundamental traits for crossing the FFI boundary:

**`IntoFFI`** - Converts Rust types to FFI-compatible representations:

pub trait IntoFFI: 'static {
    type FFI: 'static;
    fn into\_ffi(self) -> Self::FFI;
}

// Example: Converting a String to a C-compatible byte array
impl IntoFFI for Str {
    type FFI = WuiStr;
    fn into\_ffi(self) -> Self::FFI {
        WuiStr(WuiArray::new(self))
    }
}

**`IntoRust`** - Safely converts FFI types back to Rust types:

pub trait IntoRust {
    type Rust;
    unsafe fn into\_rust(self) -> Self::Rust;
}

// Example: Converting C byte array back to String
impl IntoRust for WuiStr {
    type Rust = Str;
    unsafe fn into\_rust(self) -> Self::Rust {
        let bytes = unsafe { self.0.into\_rust() };
        unsafe { Str::from\_utf8\_unchecked(bytes) }
    }
}

### Opaque Types

[](#opaque-types)

For types where the internal structure isn't relevant to native code, use the `OpaqueType` trait:

impl OpaqueType for Environment {}

// Automatically implements:
// - IntoFFI converting to \*mut WuiEnv
// - IntoRust converting from \*mut WuiEnv

This pattern is used for `Environment`, `AnyView`, `Binding<T>`, and `Computed<T>`, which native code treats as opaque pointers.

### Type Identification

[](#type-identification)

The FFI layer uses `WuiTypeId` for O(1) type identification across the FFI boundary:

#\[repr(C)\]
pub struct WuiTypeId {
    pub low: u64,
    pub high: u64,
}

This uses a 128-bit FNV-1a hash of the type name, ensuring type IDs remain stable across dylib boundaries (required for the preview system which loads user code as a dylib).

Native backends use type IDs to determine which view type they're rendering:

let viewId \= waterui\_view\_id(view)

if viewId \== waterui\_text\_id() {
    let textConfig \= waterui\_force\_as\_text(view)
    return Text(textConfig.content.get())
} else if viewId \== waterui\_button\_id() {
    // ...
}

### View Rendering Protocol

[](#view-rendering-protocol)

Native backends traverse the view tree using these core functions:

1.  **`waterui_view_id(view)`** - Get the 128-bit type ID
2.  **`waterui_view_body(view, env)`** - Expand composite views into their body
3.  **`waterui_force_as_<type>(view)`** - Downcast to specific view type (Button, Text, etc.)
4.  **`waterui_view_stretch_axis(view)`** - Query layout behavior

Composite views (user-defined) are recursively expanded via `body()`. Leaf views (Text, Button, Image) are downcast and mapped directly to native widgets.

## Reactive System FFI

[](#reactive-system-ffi)

WaterUI's reactive primitives (`Binding`, `Computed`) cross the FFI boundary with full functionality:

### Binding (Read/Write Reactive State)

[](#binding-readwrite-reactive-state)

// Rust side
let counter = Binding::int(42);

// FFI functions generated by ffi\_binding! macro:
// - waterui\_read\_binding\_i32(binding) -> i32
// - waterui\_set\_binding\_i32(binding, value)
// - waterui\_watch\_binding\_i32(binding, watcher) -> guard
// - waterui\_drop\_binding\_i32(binding)

Native code can read, write, and subscribe to changes:

let binding: UnsafeMutablePointer<WuiBinding<Int32\>\>
let value \= waterui\_read\_binding\_i32(binding)
waterui\_set\_binding\_i32(binding, value + 1)

// Watch for changes
let guard \= waterui\_watch\_binding\_i32(binding) { newValue, metadata in
    Logger.waterui.info("Counter changed to \\(newValue)")
}

### Computed (Read-Only Derived State)

[](#computed-read-only-derived-state)

// Rust side
let doubled = counter.map(|n| n \* 2);

// FFI functions generated by ffi\_computed! macro:
// - waterui\_read\_computed\_i32(computed) -> i32
// - waterui\_watch\_computed\_i32(computed, watcher) -> guard
// - waterui\_drop\_computed\_i32(computed)

Computed values can also be created from native code using `waterui_new_computed_<type>()`, enabling native-driven reactivity.

## Architecture

[](#architecture)

### Data Flow

[](#data-flow)

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Rust Application (waterui)                         │
│ - View tree definition                             │
│ - Reactive state (Binding, Computed)               │
│ - Business logic                                    │
└─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                  │ .into_ffi()
                  ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ FFI Layer (waterui-ffi)                            │
│ - Entry points: waterui_init(), waterui_app()      │
│ - Type conversion: IntoFFI, IntoRust               │
│ - View traversal: waterui_view_id(), _body()       │
│ - Reactive primitives: Binding, Computed FFI       │
└─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                  │ C ABI (waterui.h)
                  ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Native Backend (Swift/Kotlin)                      │
│ - Apple: UIView/NSView                             │
│ - Android: Android View                            │
│ - Maps Rust views to platform widgets               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Component FFI Modules

[](#component-ffi-modules)

The `components/` directory contains FFI bindings for each UI component category:

-   **`layout`** - HStack, VStack, ZStack, ScrollView, Spacer
-   **`button`** - Button with styles (plain, bordered, link)
-   **`text`** - Text rendering, fonts, styled text
-   **`form`** - TextField, SecureField, Toggle, Slider, Picker
-   **`navigation`** - NavigationStack, TabView, NavigationLink
-   **`media`** - Image, Video, Audio, LivePhoto
-   **`list`** - List, ForEach, LazyVStack
-   **`table`** - Table with columns and rows
-   **`progress`** - ProgressView, ProgressIndicator
-   **`gpu_surface`** - High-performance wgpu rendering surface

Each module defines:

1.  C-compatible struct representations (e.g., `WuiButton`)
2.  `IntoFFI` implementations for converting Rust view configs
3.  FFI view macros generating type ID and downcast functions

### Helper Macros

[](#helper-macros)

The crate provides several code generation macros to reduce boilerplate:

**`opaque!(Name, RustType, ident)`** - Generate opaque pointer FFI for a type:

opaque!(WuiEnv, waterui::Environment, env);
// Generates: WuiEnv wrapper, IntoFFI, IntoRust, waterui\_drop\_env()

**`ffi_view!(RustView, FFIStruct, ident)`** - Generate view FFI functions:

ffi\_view!(ButtonConfig, WuiButton, button);
// Generates: waterui\_button\_id(), waterui\_force\_as\_button()

**`ffi_reactive!(Type, FFIType, ident)`** - Generate binding + computed FFI:

ffi\_reactive!(i32, i32, i32);
// Generates: read/write/watch/drop for both Binding<i32> and Computed<i32>

**`into_ffi!{}`** - Derive `IntoFFI` for structs and enums:

into\_ffi! {
    ButtonStyle,
    pub enum WuiButtonStyle {
        Plain, Bordered, Link,
    }
}

## Examples

[](#examples)

### Creating a New FFI View Type

[](#creating-a-new-ffi-view-type)

To add FFI support for a new view component:

// 1. Define the Rust view config (in components/controls/src/rating.rs)
pub struct RatingConfig {
    pub value: Computed<f32\>,
    pub max: f32,
    pub color: Color,
}

// 2. Add FFI bindings (in ffi/src/components/controls.rs)
use crate::{IntoFFI, reactive::WuiComputed, color::WuiColor};

into\_ffi! {
    RatingConfig,
    pub struct WuiRating {
        value: \*mut WuiComputed<f32\>,
        max: f32,
        color: \*mut WuiColor,
    }
}

ffi\_view!(RatingConfig, WuiRating, rating);

// 3. Regenerate waterui.h
// cargo run --bin generate\_header --features cbindgen --manifest-path ffi/Cargo.toml

// 4. Implement in Swift (backends/apple/Sources/WaterUI/Views/Rating.swift)
// if viewId == waterui\_rating\_id() {
//     let config = waterui\_force\_as\_rating(view)
//     return RatingView(config: config)
// }

### Implementing Custom Reactive Properties

[](#implementing-custom-reactive-properties)

// Generate FFI for a custom type in reactive state
use waterui::color::Color;

ffi\_reactive!(Color, \*mut WuiColor, color);
// Now Binding<Color> and Computed<Color> can cross FFI

### Creating Native-Controlled Computed Values

[](#creating-native-controlled-computed-values)

// Swift side creates a computed that Rust can read
let computed = waterui\_new\_computed\_i32(
    dataPtr,
    { ptr in return getCurrentValue(ptr) },
    { ptr, watcher in return watchValue(ptr, watcher) },
    { ptr in cleanup(ptr) }
)

// Pass to Rust view
let text = waterui\_text(computed)

## C Header Generation

[](#c-header-generation)

The crate includes a `generate_header` binary that uses `cbindgen` to produce `waterui.h`:

cargo run --bin generate\_header --features cbindgen --manifest-path ffi/Cargo.toml

This generates the C header and automatically copies it to:

-   `backends/apple/Sources/CWaterUI/include/waterui.h` (SwiftUI backend)
-   `backends/android/runtime/src/main/cpp/waterui.h` (Android backend)

The header is checked into version control, and CI verifies it's always up-to-date with the Rust code.

## Native Backend Render Pipeline

[](#native-backend-render-pipeline)

Native backends (Android, Apple, etc.) must follow a specific initialization sequence when rendering WaterUI views.

### Required Sequence

[](#required-sequence)

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. waterui_init()                                                   │
│    - Initializes panic hooks and global executors                   │
│    - Returns an Environment pointer                                 │
│    - MUST be called first before any other waterui_* functions      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Theme installation (recommended)                                 │
│    - Install appearance: waterui_theme_install_color_scheme()       │
│    - Install colors:     waterui_theme_install_color()              │
│    - Install fonts:      waterui_theme_install_font()               │
│    - Legacy: waterui_env_install_theme() is deprecated              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. waterui_app(env)                                                 │
│    - Creates the application from user's app(env) function          │
│    - Returns WuiApp with windows and environment                    │
│    - MUST be called AFTER waterui_init() and theme installation     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 4. Render Loop (for each view)                                      │
│    a. waterui_view_id(view) → Get the type ID                       │
│    b. Check if it's a "raw view" (Text, Button, etc.)               │
│       - If raw: waterui_force_as_*(view) → Extract native data      │
│       - If composite: waterui_view_body(view, env) → Get body view  │
│    c. Render the native widget or recurse into body                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Raw Views vs Composite Views

[](#raw-views-vs-composite-views)

WaterUI distinguishes between two kinds of views:

-   **Raw Views**: Leaf components that map directly to native widgets. Examples: `Text`, `Button`, `Color`, `TextField`, `Toggle`, `Slider`, `Stepper`, `Progress`, `Spacer`, `Picker`, `ScrollView`.
    
-   **Composite Views**: User-defined views that have a `body()` method returning other views. When you encounter a view that isn't in the raw view registry, call `waterui_view_body(view, env)` to get its body and continue rendering recursively.
    

## Features

[](#features)

-   **`std`** (default) - Enable standard library support
-   **`cbindgen`** - Required for the `generate_header` binary

## API Overview

[](#api-overview)

### Core Entry Points

[](#core-entry-points)

-   `waterui_init()` - Initialize runtime and return Environment
-   `waterui_app(env)` - Create application from user's app() function
-   `waterui_clone_env(env)` - Clone Environment for child contexts

### View Traversal

[](#view-traversal)

-   `waterui_view_id(view)` - Get type ID as 128-bit value
-   `waterui_view_body(view, env)` - Expand composite view to its body
-   `waterui_view_stretch_axis(view)` - Query layout stretch behavior
-   `waterui_anyview_id()` - Get AnyView type ID

### Type Downcasting

[](#type-downcasting)

-   `waterui_force_as_<type>(view)` - Downcast to specific view type
-   `waterui_<type>_id()` - Get type ID for comparison

### Reactive Primitives

[](#reactive-primitives)

-   `waterui_read_binding_<type>(binding)` - Read current value
-   `waterui_set_binding_<type>(binding, value)` - Update value
-   `waterui_watch_binding_<type>(binding, watcher)` - Subscribe to changes
-   `waterui_read_computed_<type>(computed)` - Read derived value
-   `waterui_watch_computed_<type>(computed, watcher)` - Subscribe to changes
-   `waterui_new_computed_<type>(...)` - Create native-controlled computed
-   `waterui_drop_binding_<type>(binding)` - Cleanup binding
-   `waterui_drop_computed_<type>(computed)` - Cleanup computed

### Memory Management

[](#memory-management)

-   `waterui_drop_<type>(ptr)` - Free resource of given type
-   `waterui_drop_retain(retain)` - Drop retained value

## Safety Considerations

[](#safety-considerations)

The FFI layer involves extensive `unsafe` code by necessity:

1.  **Pointer Validity**: Callers must ensure pointers from FFI functions remain valid for their usage
2.  **Ownership Transfer**: Functions taking `*mut T` typically take ownership and will free the memory
3.  **Thread Safety**: `waterui_init()` must be called once on the main thread only
4.  **Type Downcasting**: `waterui_force_as_*()` functions assume the view type matches

Native backends are responsible for:

-   Properly managing the lifetimes of FFI pointers
-   Calling drop functions when resources are no longer needed
-   Not using pointers after they've been consumed

## Performance

[](#performance)

The FFI layer is designed for zero-overhead abstraction:

-   **Type IDs**: O(1) comparison (128-bit integer equality)
-   **View Traversal**: Single pointer dereference per level
-   **Reactive Updates**: Direct function pointer callbacks, no allocation
-   **Arrays**: Zero-copy views into Rust data via vtable-based slicing

The reactive system uses reference counting (`Rc`) on the Rust side and lets native code subscribe via lightweight watcher callbacks.

## Development Workflow

[](#development-workflow)

When adding a new view type to WaterUI:

1.  Define the Rust view struct in the appropriate component crate
2.  Add FFI bindings in `ffi/src/components/<module>.rs`
3.  Regenerate the C header: `cargo run --bin generate_header --features cbindgen --manifest-path ffi/Cargo.toml`
4.  Implement the native renderer in Swift (`backends/apple`) and Kotlin (`backends/android`)
5.  Update tests to verify FFI contract

The workflow ensures Rust, C header, and native backends stay synchronized.

## License

[](#license)

MIT

Let me think about the key architectural facts:

**Pathland**:
- Protocol-first, binary 16-byte opcode stream
- Engine emits declarative structure (TREE + STYLE opcodes) into a shared-memory ring buffer
- Diff-based reactive emission (deltas only)
- Renderer is stateless: pure function of opcode stream, retains only its rendered-output tree
- Both directions binary (EVENT ring for input)
- No virtual tree diff? No — actually Pathland IS diff-based (retained tree + diff-based emission). Wait, actually Pathland is a retained tree + diff-based reactive emitter.
- no_std + wasm32 core
- Native elements everywhere, renderer maps opcodes to native widgets
- Design tokens: renderer-owned
- Catalog-driven codegen for other languages (YAML → Java)

**WaterUI**:
- Rust-first cross-platform UI framework
- View trait, declarative composition (body)
- Fine-grained reactivity (nami): Binding/Computed, precise per-signal updates, NO virtual tree diff, no structural diff
- FFI layer: C ABI bridge; native backend traverses view tree via waterui_view_id / waterui_view_body / waterui_force_as_*
- Native backends map Rust views to native widgets (UIKit/AppKit/Android View/GTK4)
- Also self-drawn renderers (Hydrolysis GPU via Vello, Dew CPU)
- Theme tokens, Environment DI
- Raw views vs composite views

Now: "How would Pathland's opcode engine fit into WaterUI?"

Key insight: They occupy different layers but have overlapping conceptual goals. Pathland is a *protocol/transport* between an application core and a renderer; WaterUI is a full framework where the Rust core and native backends already communicate via a C ABI (FFI). The FFI layer in WaterUI is analogous to Pathland's opcode engine + transport + native C-ABI shim.

Where could Pathland's opcode engine fit? Several angles:

1. **As a replacement for the FFI traversal protocol.** WaterUI currently uses a pull-based, function-call FFI: the backend walks the view tree (waterui_view_body recursion), downcasts (force_as_*), and watches bindings via function-pointer callbacks. Pathland is push-based: the engine emits a flat, diffed stream of 16-byte opcodes into a ring buffer. Fitting Pathland here would mean replacing the "walk the tree + downcast + watch" protocol with a "drain a diffed opcode stream" protocol.

2. **Tension: reactivity model differs fundamentally.**
   - WaterUI's nami: precise per-signal, fine-grained, no structural diff, no virtual tree. A Binding change directly invokes the watcher on the native side (waterui_watch_binding_*). Updates are "surgical".
   - Pathland: diff-based reactive emission from a retained tree — the engine reconciles a marked-dirty tree and emits deltas (TREE create/delete/insert/move + STYLE SET_PROPERTY/SET_TEXT). This is closer to SwiftUI-style structural diff + property diffs.
   
   So Pathland's diff-based emission is philosophically at odds with WaterUI's "no virtual tree to diff" fine-grained model. WaterUI explicitly rejects structural diff. Pathland's AGENTS.md says "diff-based reactive emission". This is a real architectural conflict.

3. **Where it fits naturally: as a *backend* / transport alternative, or as a serialization layer for remote projection.**
   - Pathland's transport (network batch encode/decode) could be a remote-rendering path: e.g., projecting a WaterUI view tree to a browser/remote host over a binary protocol. WaterUI's planned future includes web/remote. Pathland's opcode format could be the wire format.
   - Pathland's self-drawn renderer mapping (opcodes → native elements) is similar to what Hydrolysis/Dew do (retained tree → Vello/cpu draw).

4. **As a decoupling layer between WaterUI core and its backends.** Pathland's stateless-renderer principle and "renderer is a pure function of the opcode stream" could formalize WaterUI's backend contract. But WaterUI already has a backend contract (the FFI). Pathland's value-add is: language-agnostic binary stream (not a C ABI you must link), a ring buffer (zero-copy), and a *formal spec* (OPCODE.md + conformance vectors).

5. **Concretely, the natural insertion point is the FFI layer (waterui-ffi).** Replace/augment the function-call FFI with a Pathland ring + opcode emitter. The Rust side (WaterUI core) would emit the declarative view structure as opcodes, and each native backend becomes a Pathland renderer that drains the ring and maps opcodes → widgets. This is exactly Pathland's desktop architecture (pathland-view-native + pathland-render-gtk), generalized to Apple/Android.

But there's a subtlety: WaterUI's fine-grained reactivity lives on the native side via watchers (function-pointer callbacks). If we move to Pathland's push opcode model, updates become "the engine emits SET_TEXT/SET_PROPERTY opcodes when a signal changes" — which is actually compatible with WaterUI's "signal-aware" goal, but requires WaterUI's nami graph to be able to mark specific nodes dirty and emit only those. Pathland already has this (signals → re-emit only bound nodes). So there's a convergence point: both want "a signal change re-emits only the affected nodes".

Actually this is a nice observation: Pathland's signal system (node_bind_text / node_bind_property → SET_TEXT/SET_PROPERTY partial emit) is conceptually the SAME as WaterUI's fine-grained Binding/Computed → precise update. The difference is Pathland routes updates through a diffed opcode stream in a ring, while WaterUI routes updates through direct FFI watcher callbacks.

So the answer is nuanced. Let me structure it:

**Summary answer:**
Pathland's opcode engine is a *transport/protocol* layer. In WaterUI, the analogous layer is `waterui-ffi`. So the opcode engine would fit as (a) a replacement/alternative to the pull-based FFI traversal protocol, sitting between the Rust view tree and the native backends, or (b) a serialization/wire format for remote projection (web/SSR/WebSocket) and for the self-drawn renderers.

**Where it fits (concrete):**
1. **Between core and backends (the FFI boundary).** Pathland's engine + ring buffer + native C-ABI shim is a drop-in conceptual replacement for waterui-ffi's traversal protocol. The Rust side emits declarative TREE/STYLE opcodes; each backend drains and maps to widgets. Pros: language-agnostic (no cbindgen header, no per-type waterui_force_as_*), zero-copy ring, formal spec + conformance vectors, stateless-renderer enforcement. Cons: loses WaterUI's fine-grained nami watcher callbacks unless you re-implement "signal → partial opcode emit", and adds a second source-of-truth registry (opcode catalog) alongside the View trait.

2. **As a serialization format for the network/remote backend** (WaterUI's future web/remote projection). Pathland's network-batch transport already exists; this is the cleanest fit — serialize the view tree + deltas for SSR/WebSocket/remote.

3. **As the command protocol for the self-drawn renderers (Hydrolysis/Dew).** Hydrolysis re-encodes a retained scene; Dew does dirty-region CPU raster. Pathland's "dirty-region/diff" model matches Dew well; but Hydrolysis explicitly forbids damage tracking. Pathland's diff-based emission aligns with Dew, conflicts with Hydrolysis's whole-scene philosophy.

**Where it doesn't fit / tensions:**
- **Diff-based emission vs fine-grained reactivity.** Pathland reconciles a retained tree and emits structural diffs; WaterUI's principle #8 forbids structural diff and mandates per-signal updates. To fit, Pathland would need to be used in a mode that only ever emits SET_PROPERTY/SET_TEXT (no structural TREE ops) — i.e., its signal path — and WaterUI would have to give up some of nami's directness. This is the biggest conflict.
- **Catalog-driven static DSL vs dynamic View trait.** Pathland's opcode IDs are a fixed catalog (constants.rs); WaterUI's views are Rust types with 128-bit type IDs (FNV hash). Pathland's fixed catalog is less extensible than WaterUI's type system; WaterUI's principle #2 (minimum FFI surface, compose in Rust) pushes toward composition, whereas Pathland's catalog enumerates components.
- **Statelessness enforcement** is a philosophical bonus Pathland brings, but WaterUI already treats backends as dumb mappers; Pathland's "renderer must not retain state" is compatible.

**Recommendation:** The most natural, non-invasive fit is as a *wire/transport format* (option 2), and possibly as an alternative *backend contract* for non-native/remote renderers. Retrofitting it as the primary FFI would require reconciling the reactivity models — likely by mapping WaterUI's Binding/Computed signals onto Pathland's signal-binding + partial-emit path and dropping the structural-diff path.

156:     debug_assert!(slots.is_power_of_two());
157:     slots - 1
158: }

160: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
161: // Guest (producer)
162: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
163: 
164: /// Producer side: the guest engine writing opcodes and arena data into shared
165: /// linear memory. Owns the header, ring, and arena regions as disjoint slices.
166: pub struct Guest<'a> {
167:     header: &'a mut [u8],
168:     slots: &'a mut [u8],
169:     /// Host → guest event ring (guest reads raw inputs here).
170:     event_slots: &'a mut [u8],
171:     arena: &'a mut [u8],
172:     /// Write cursor captured at `begin_frame`.
173:     frame_start: u32,
174: }
175: 
176: impl<'a> Guest<'a> {
177:     /// Create a guest view over the linear memory. `init_memory` MUST have been
178:     /// called on the same memory beforehand.
179:     pub fn new(mem: &'a mut [u8], layout: &MemoryLayout) -> Self {
180:         let (header, rest) = mem.split_at_mut(memory::HEADER_SIZE);
181:         let (slots, rest) = rest.split_at_mut(layout.ring_bytes());
182:         let (event_slots, arena) = rest.split_at_mut(layout.event_ring_bytes());
183:         let frame_start = header::get_u32(header, OFF_WRITE_CURSOR);
184:         Self {
185:             header,
186:             slots,
187:             event_slots,
188:             arena,
189:             frame_start,
190:         }
191:     }
192: 
193:     fn mask(&self) -> usize {
194:         slot_mask(self.header)
195:     }
196: 
197:     /// Record the start of a new frame.
198:     pub fn begin_frame(&mut self) {
199:         self.frame_start = header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_WRITE_CURSOR);
200:     }
201: 
202:     /// Number of opcodes written since the last `begin_frame`.
203:     pub fn pending(&self) -> usize {
204:         let write = header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_WRITE_CURSOR);
205:         let mask = self.mask() as u32;
206:         (write.wrapping_sub(self.frame_start) & mask) as usize
207:     }
208: 
209:     /// End the frame: increments `frameCount`.
210:     pub fn end_frame(&mut self) {
211:         let count = header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT);
212:         header::set_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT, count.wrapping_add(1));
213:     }
214: 
215:     /// Total frames produced so far.
216:     pub fn frame_count(&self) -> u32 {
217:         header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT)
218:     }
219: 
220:     // --- TREE ---
221: 
222:     pub fn create_node(&mut self, node_id: u32, component_type: u16) -> Result<(), RingError> {
223:         ring_fn::push_create_node(self.slots, self.header, self.mask(), node_id, component_type)
224:     }
225: 
226:     pub fn delete_node(&mut self, node_id: u32) -> Result<(), RingError> {
227:         ring_fn::push_delete_node(self.slots, self.header, self.mask(), node_id)
228:     }
229: 
230:     pub fn insert_child(&mut self, parent: u32, child: u32, index: u32) -> Result<(), RingError> {
231:         ring_fn::push_insert_child(self.slots, self.header, self.mask(), parent, child, index)
232:     }
233: 
234:     pub fn remove_child(&mut self, parent: u32, child: u32) -> Result<(), RingError> {
235:         ring_fn::push_remove_child(self.slots, self.header, self.mask(), parent, child)
236:     }
237: 
238:     pub fn move_child(
239:         &mut self,
240:         parent: u32,
241:         child: u32,
242:         new_index: u32,
243:     ) -> Result<(), RingError> {
244:         ring_fn::push_move_child(self.slots, self.header, self.mask(), parent, child, new_index)
245:     }
246: 
247:     // --- STYLE ---
248: 
249:     pub fn set_property(
250:         &mut self,
251:         node_id: u32,
252:         property_id: u16,
253:         value_type: u8,
254:         value: u32,
255:     ) -> Result<(), RingError> {
256:         ring_fn::push_set_property(
257:             self.slots,
258:             self.header,
259:             self.mask(),
260:             node_id,
261:             property_id,
262:             value_type,
263:             value,
264:         )
265:     }
266: 
267:     /// Set a node's text content via the arena.
268:     pub fn set_text(&mut self, node_id: u32, text: &str) -> Result<u32, RingError> {
269:         let arena_ref = arena_fn::alloc_str(self.arena, self.header, text).map_err(|_| RingError::Full)?;
270:         ring_fn::push_set_text(self.slots, self.header, self.mask(), node_id, arena_ref)?;
271:         Ok(arena_ref)
272:     }
273: 
274:     /// Allocate arbitrary bytes into the arena, returning the offset.
275:     pub fn alloc(&mut self, bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<u32, ArenaError> {
276:         arena_fn::alloc(self.arena, self.header, bytes)
277:     }
278: 
279:     /// Allocate a string into the arena, returning the offset.
280:     pub fn alloc_str(&mut self, s: &str) -> Result<u32, ArenaError> {
281:         arena_fn::alloc_str(self.arena, self.header, s)
282:     }
283: 
284:     // --- META ---
285: 
286:     pub fn reset(&mut self) -> Result<(), RingError> {
287:         ring_fn::push_reset(self.slots, self.header, self.mask())
288:     }
289: 
290:     // --- EVENT ingress (host → guest) ---
291: 
292:     /// Drain all pending raw-input events written by the host into the event
293:     /// ring, decoding each 16-byte `EVENT` opcode into a typed [`Event`].
294:     ///
295:     /// The guest (app/engine) polls this to receive renderer-reported inputs.
296:     pub fn drain_events(&mut self) -> Vec<Event> {
297:         let mask = self.mask();
298:         let ops = ring_fn::read_events(&self.event_slots, self.header, mask);
299:         ops.into_iter()
300:             .filter_map(|op| Event::try_from(op).ok())
301:             .collect()
302:     }
303: }
304: 
305: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
306: // Host (consumer)
307: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
308: 
309: /// A completed frame produced by the guest: a sequence of opcodes plus arena
310: /// access.
311: ///
312: /// `Frame` is the **transport seam**: both the shared-memory ring (`Host`) and
313: /// network batch decoders produce frame views, so consumers such as
314: /// `RenderTree::apply_frame` work identically regardless of origin.
315: pub struct Frame<'a> {
316:     slots: &'a [u8],
317:     arena: &'a [u8],
318:     start: usize,
319:     end: usize,
320: }
321: 
322: impl<'a> Frame<'a> {
323:     /// Construct a frame view over contiguous 16-byte opcode slots plus an
324:     /// arena region (`start`/`end` are byte offsets into `slots`).
325:     ///
326:     /// Used by transport backends to produce `Frame` views over their own
327:     /// buffers; `Host` builds these internally from the ring.
328:     pub fn from_parts(slots: &'a [u8], arena: &'a [u8], start: usize, end: usize) -> Self {
329:         Self {
330:             slots,
331:             arena,
332:             start,
333:             end,
334:         }
335:     }
336: 
337:     /// Iterate the opcodes in this frame, in order.
338:     pub fn opcodes(&self) -> FrameIter<'a> {
339:         FrameIter {
340:             slots: self.slots,
341:             cursor: self.start,
342:             end: self.end,
343:         }
344:     }
345: 
346:     /// Number of opcodes in the frame.
347:     pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
348:         (self.end - self.start) / Opcode::SIZE
349:     }
350: 
351:     pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
352:         self.len() == 0
353:     }
354: 
355:     /// Read an arena entry by offset (see `Guest::alloc` / `Guest::alloc_str`).
356:     pub fn arena_get(&self, offset: u32) -> Result<&'a [u8], ArenaError> {
357:         arena_fn::get(self.arena, offset)
358:     }
359: 
360:     /// Read an arena string by offset.
361:     pub fn arena_str(&self, offset: u32) -> Result<&'a str, ArenaError> {
362:         arena_fn::get_str(self.arena, offset)
363:     }
364: 
365:     /// The full arena region (for transport serialization of arena deltas).
366:     pub fn arena(&self) -> &'a [u8] {
367:         self.arena
368:     }
369: }
370: 
371: /// Iterator over the opcodes in a `Frame`.
372: pub struct FrameIter<'a> {
373:     slots: &'a [u8],
374:     cursor: usize,
375:     end: usize,
376: }
377: 
378: impl<'a> Iterator for FrameIter<'a> {
379:     type Item = Opcode;
380: 
381:     fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Opcode> {
382:         if self.cursor >= self.end {
383:             return None;
384:         }
385:         let bytes: [u8; 16] = self.slots[self.cursor..self.cursor + 16].try_into().unwrap();
386:         self.cursor += 16;
387:         Some(Opcode::from_bytes(&bytes))
388:     }
389: }
390: 
391: /// Consumer side: the host renderer reading completed frames.
392: ///
393: /// SPSC contract: the host never reads past the producer's published
394: /// `writeCursor`, and the producer never overwrites an unconsumed `readCursor`.
395: /// If the host is slow, multiple produced frames are coalesced into one `Frame`
396: /// (opcodes remain in order); the `frameCount` simply signals "new data".
397: pub struct Host<'a> {
398:     header: &'a mut [u8],
399:     slots: &'a [u8],
400:     /// Host → guest event ring (host writes raw inputs here).
401:     event_slots: &'a mut [u8],
402:     arena: &'a [u8],
403:     /// Number of frames already consumed by this host view.
404:     consumed: u32,
405: }
406: 
407: impl<'a> Host<'a> {
408:     /// Create a host view over the linear memory.
409:     pub fn new(mem: &'a mut [u8], layout: &MemoryLayout) -> Self {
410:         let (header, rest) = mem.split_at_mut(memory::HEADER_SIZE);
411:         let (slots, rest) = rest.split_at_mut(layout.ring_bytes());
412:         let (event_slots, arena) = rest.split_at_mut(layout.event_ring_bytes());
413:         let slots: &'a [u8] = slots;
414:         let arena: &'a [u8] = arena;
415:         Self {
416:             header,
417:             slots,
418:             event_slots,
419:             arena,
420:             consumed: 0,
421:         }
422:     }
423: 
424:     /// Total frames produced by the guest (for diagnostics).
425:     pub fn frame_count(&self) -> u32 {
426:         header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT)
427:     }
428: 
429:     /// Consume all frames produced since the last call, advancing `readCursor`.
430:     ///
431:     /// Returns at most one `Frame` (all new opcodes since the last drain). If
432:     /// the producer produced multiple frames before this call they coalesce.
433:     pub fn frames(&mut self) -> Vec<Frame<'a>> {
434:         let frame_count = header::get_u32(self.header, OFF_FRAME_COUNT);
435:         if self.consumed >= frame_count {
436:             return Vec::new();
437:         }
438:         let mask = slot_mask(self.header);
439:         let start = ring_fn::cursor(self.header, OFF_READ_CURSOR, mask);
440:         let end = ring_fn::cursor(self.header, OFF_WRITE_CURSOR, mask);
441: 
442:         // The POC producer flushes before the ring fills, so `end >= start`
443:         // always holds. Guard against a wrapped ring by draining nothing; a
444:         // wrapped producer must flush first (see OPCODE.md backpressure).
445:         if end < start {
446:             return Vec::new();
447:         }
448: 
449:         // No new opcodes since the last drain (readCursor == writeCursor). This
450:         // also covers a freshly-created host view whose `consumed` counter
451:         // starts at 0 but whose cursors have already been drained by an earlier
452:         // view — without this, `next_frame` would return empty frames forever.
453:         if start == end {
454:             return Vec::new();
455:         }
456: 
457:         let frames = vec![Frame {
458:             slots: self.slots,
459:             arena: self.arena,
460:             start: start * Opcode::SIZE,
461:             end: end * Opcode::SIZE,
462:         }];
463: 
464:         header::set_u32(self.header, OFF_READ_CURSOR, end as u32);
465:         self.consumed = frame_count;
466:         frames
467:     }
468: 
469:     /// Write a raw-input event (host → guest) into the event ring, encoded as a
470:     /// 16-byte `EVENT` opcode. The renderer reports inputs here; the guest
471:     /// drains them via [`Guest::drain_events`].
472:     pub fn send_event(&mut self, event: &Event) -> Result<(), RingError> {
473:         let mask = slot_mask(self.header);
474:         ring_fn::push_event(self.event_slots, self.header, mask, &event.encode())
475:     }
476: }

478: #[cfg(test)]
479: mod tests {
480:     use super::*;
481:     use crate::constants::{category, component_type, property_id, value_type};
482:     use alloc::vec;
483: 
484:     #[test]
485:     fn guest_host_round_trip() {
486:         let layout = MemoryLayout::default();
487:         let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
488:         init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);
489: 
490:         let mut guest = Guest::new(&mut mem, &layout);
491:         guest.begin_frame();
492:         guest.create_node(1, component_type::VSTACK).unwrap();
493:         guest.insert_child(0, 1, APPEND).unwrap();
494:         guest.set_property(1, property_id::SPACING, value_type::F32, 4.0f32.to_bits()).unwrap();
495:         guest
496:             .set_property(1, property_id::PADDING, value_type::F32, 8.0f32.to_bits())
497:             .unwrap();
498:         let arena_ref = guest.set_text(1, "Hello").unwrap();
499:         assert_eq!(guest.pending(), 5);
500:         guest.end_frame();
501:         assert_eq!(guest.frame_count(), 1);
502: 
503:         let mut host = Host::new(&mut mem, &layout);
504:         assert_eq!(host.frame_count(), 1);
505:         let frames = host.frames();
506:         assert_eq!(frames.len(), 1);
507:         let frame = &frames[0];
508:         let ops: Vec<Opcode> = frame.opcodes().collect();
509:         assert_eq!(ops.len(), 5);
510:         assert_eq!(ops[0].category(), category::TREE);
511:         assert_eq!(ops[0].a(), 1);
512:         assert_eq!(ops[1].a(), 0); // parent root
513:         assert_eq!(ops[2].b() as u16, property_id::SPACING);
514:         assert_eq!(ops[2].c_f32(), 4.0);
515:         assert_eq!(frame.arena_str(arena_ref).unwrap(), "Hello");
516:         // Second drain is empty.
517:         assert!(host.frames().is_empty());
518:     }

520:     #[test]
521:     fn ring_full_is_reported() {
522:         let mut layout = MemoryLayout::default();

524:         let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];

527:         let mut guest = Guest::new(&mut mem, &layout);
528:         // 4 slots -> capacity is slot_count-1 = 3 opcodes before full.
529:         assert!(guest.create_node(1, component_type::VSTACK).is_ok());

531:         assert!(guest.create_node(3, component_type::TEXT).is_ok());
532:         assert_eq!(
533:             guest.create_node(4, component_type::TEXT).unwrap_err(),
534:             RingError::Full
535:         );
536:     }
537: 
538:     #[test]
539:     fn host_event_round_trips_to_guest() {
540:         let layout = MemoryLayout::default();
541:         let mut mem = vec![0u8; layout.total_bytes()];
542:         init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);
543: 
544:         // Host (renderer) writes an event.
545:         let mut host = Host::new(&mut mem, &layout);
546:         host.send_event(&Event::PointerUp {
547:             target: 4,
548:             x: 10.0,
549:             y: 20.0,
550:             secondary: false,
551:         })
552:         .unwrap();
553:         drop(host);
554: 
555:         // Guest drains and decodes it.
556:         let mut guest = Guest::new(&mut mem, &layout);
557:         let events = guest.drain_events();
558:         assert_eq!(
559:             events,
560:             vec![Event::PointerUp {
561:                 target: 4,
562:                 x: 10.0,
563:                 y: 20.0,

565:             }]
566:         );
567:         // Second drain is empty.
568:         assert!(guest.drain_events().is_empty());
569:     }

575:         init_memory(&mut mem, &layout);

1: //! The fixed-size 16-byte Pathland opcode.
2: //!
3: //! Layout (see `spec/OPCODE.md`):
4: //!
5: //! ```text
6: //! [Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]
7: //! ```
8: //!
9: //! All multi-byte fields are little-endian on the wire. `size_of::<Opcode>() == 16`,
10: //! so a 64-byte cache line holds exactly 4 opcodes.
11: 
12: use core::ptr;
13: 
14: /// Size of one opcode in bytes.
15: pub const OPCODE_SIZE: usize = 16;
16: 
17: /// A fixed-size 16-byte opcode.
18: ///
19: /// This struct intentionally mirrors the wire layout and is `#[repr(C, packed)]`
20: /// per the specification. Because it is packed, fields may be unaligned; always
21: /// read fields through the accessor methods (which use unaligned reads) rather
22: /// than by value.
23: #[repr(C, packed)]
24: #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
25: pub struct Opcode {
26:     /// Opcode category (see `constants::Category`).
27:     pub category: u8,
28:     /// Command within the category (see `constants::Command*`).
29:     pub command: u8,
30:     /// Category/command-specific flags.
31:     pub flags: u16,
32:     /// Primary payload.
33:     pub a: u32,
34:     /// Secondary payload.
35:     pub b: u32,
36:     /// Tertiary payload.
37:     pub c: u32,
38: }
39: 
40: impl Opcode {
41:     /// Byte size of an opcode (`16`).
42:     pub const SIZE: usize = OPCODE_SIZE;
43: 
44:     /// Construct an opcode from raw fields.
45:     #[inline]
46:     pub const fn new(category: u8, command: u8, flags: u16, a: u32, b: u32, c: u32) -> Self {
47:         Self {
48:             category,
49:             command,
50:             flags,
51:             a,
52:             b,
53:             c,
54:         }
55:     }
56: 
57:     /// The opcode category.
58:     #[inline]
59:     pub fn category(&self) -> u8 {
60:         self.category
61:     }
62: 
63:     /// The command within the category.
64:     #[inline]
65:     pub fn command(&self) -> u8 {

67:     }

113:     }

115:     /// Serialize to the 16-byte wire representation (little-endian).
116:     pub fn to_bytes(&self) -> [u8; OPCODE_SIZE] {
117:         let mut out = [0u8; OPCODE_SIZE];
118:         out[0] = self.category;
119:         out[1] = self.command;
120:         // SAFETY: read_unaligned is well-defined for packed fields.
121:         let flags = unsafe { ptr::addr_of!(self.flags).read_unaligned() };
122:         let a = unsafe { ptr::addr_of!(self.a).read_unaligned() };
123:         let b = unsafe { ptr::addr_of!(self.b).read_unaligned() };
124:         let c = unsafe { ptr::addr_of!(self.c).read_unaligned() };
125:         out[2..4].copy_from_slice(&flags.to_le_bytes());
126:         out[4..8].copy_from_slice(&a.to_le_bytes());
127:         out[8..12].copy_from_slice(&b.to_le_bytes());
128:         out[12..16].copy_from_slice(&c.to_le_bytes());
129:         out
130:     }

132:     /// Deserialize from the 16-byte wire representation (little-endian).
133:     pub fn from_bytes(bytes: &[u8; OPCODE_SIZE]) -> Self {
134:         let category = bytes[0];
135:         let command = bytes[1];
136:         let flags = u16::from_le_bytes([bytes[2], bytes[3]]);
137:         let a = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[4..8].try_into().unwrap());
138:         let b = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[8..12].try_into().unwrap());
139:         let c = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[12..16].try_into().unwrap());
140:         Self {
141:             category,
142:             command,
143:             flags,
144:             a,
145:             b,
146:             c,
147:         }
148:     }

1: //! # pathland-core-transport
2: //!
3: //! How Pathland opcodes are transported from the guest engine to host
4: //! renderers. There are two peer backends:
5: //!
6: //! - **Shared memory** (desktop/native): the ring buffer + arena in
7: //!   `pathland-core` (`Guest`/`Host`). Zero-copy. This crate treats it as
8: //!   the local transport — no duplication.
9: //! - **Network batch** (SSR → browser): opcodes + arena data serialized into
10: //!   **batches**, flushed on a **time interval** or a **network-frame size**
11: //!   (whichever comes first).
12: //!
13: //! `pathland_core::Frame` is the **transport seam**: the renderer's
14: //! `RenderTree::apply_frame` consumes frames regardless of origin. `BatchDecoder`
15: //! produces `Frame` views over decoded batches, so a network batch feeds the
16: //! renderer exactly like a shared-memory frame.
17: //!
18: //! ## Batch wire format
19: //!
20: //! ```text
21: //! magic "PLPL" (u32 LE) | version (u16) | flags (u16) | frameCount (u32)
22: //! | opcodeCount (u32) | opcodes (16 B × opcodeCount) | arenaDeltaLen (u32)
23: //! | arena delta bytes
24: //! ```
25: //!
26: //! The arena is append-only (bump); batches carry only the bytes appended since
27: //! the previous batch. The decoder appends them to a mirrored arena, so absolute
28: //! `arenaRef` offsets stay valid — exactly as in shared memory.
29: //!
30: //! ## Example (producer)
31: //!
32: //! ```no_run
33: //! use pathland_core_transport::{Batcher, BatchPolicy, BatchEncoder};
34: //! use std::time::Duration;
35: //!
36: //! let policy = BatchPolicy::new(Duration::from_millis(4), 1400);
37: //! let mut batcher = Batcher::new(policy);
38: //! let mut encoder = BatchEncoder::new();
39: //!
40: //! // batcher.push_frame(&frame) accumulates opcodes + arena delta;
41: //! // batcher.flush() -> Option<Vec<u8>> produces the serialized batch.
42: //! ```
43:

parts.text:
Now I have a clear picture of the Pathland source. The key finding: `pathland-core` is actually nicely layered:

- `opcode.rs` — pure 16-byte Opcode struct + encode/decode. Zero deps.
- `ring.rs` — ring push functions (the raw opcode ring, `ring_fn::push_*`).
- `arena.rs` — bump arena.
- `memory.rs` — MemoryLayout, header offsets.
- `constants.rs` — category/command/component_type/property_id/value_type.
- `events.rs` — Event encode/decode.
- `engine.rs` — the diff-based emitter (retained tree → opcodes). THIS is the "diff" part.
- `node.rs` — retained tree types (Node/Component).
- `signal.rs` — signals.

And crucially, the "Guest" (producer) is essentially a thin wrapper over `ring_fn::push_*` — it just writes opcodes into the ring. The `Engine` (in engine.rs) is what *decides* what opcodes to emit via diffing. So the "core opcode part" (opcode.rs + ring.rs + arena.rs + memory.rs + constants.rs + events.rs) is genuinely separable from the "engine/diff" part (engine.rs + node.rs + signal.rs). The Guest already exposes the raw push API (`create_node`, `set_property`, `set_text`, etc.) independent of Engine.

So the user's plan is actually very clean and well-aligned with the existing crate structure. The Guest/Host + ring + arena + opcode + constants + events + memory is exactly "core opcode part with transport", and it's decoupled from `Engine` (diff), `node` (retained tree), and `signal`.

The transport crate (`pathland-core-transport`) is also clean: `RingTransport` (shared-memory ring owner), `BatchEncoder`/`BatchDecoder` (network batch), `Batcher`/`BatchPolicy` (time/size batching), plus traits `DriverTransport`, `FrameSource`, `InputSink`.

Now the question: could they add Pathland's opcode engine as a new backend in WaterUI and benefit from all the rest WaterUI has to offer?

Answer: Yes, and the framing is clean. Let me be precise.

The "backend" in WaterUI terms = a renderer that consumes the WaterUI view tree. But Pathland's opcode engine + transport is not a renderer; it's a *serialization/transport layer*. So "adding Pathland as a backend" really means adding a backend whose render side is: convert WaterUI's view tree into a Pathland opcode stream, emit into a ring (or network batch), and let a Pathland renderer consume it.

Actually, wait — there are two ways to read "backend":

(1) **Pathland as a WaterUI backend** = a new entry under `backends/pathland` that renders WaterUI views *through* Pathland opcodes → a Pathland renderer. This is a "portable/self-drawn realization" in WaterUI's taxonomy (principle #4), sitting alongside hydrolysis/dew/gtk. The value: reuse WaterUI's DSL + reactivity + components, get Pathland's protocol/transport/remote-reach.

(2) The inverse — but the user clearly said "add pathland opcode engine as a new backend in waterui", so it's (1).

Now, what does "benefit from all the rest WaterUI has to offer" mean? WaterUI offers: the View trait + declarative composition, the component library (form derive, navigation, media, gestures, markdown, charts), Environment/theme tokens, fine-grained reactivity (nami Binding/Computed), the CLI (water create/run/preview), previews (render to PNG), testing (semantic accessibility tree via waterui-testing). 

The key architectural question is: **what WaterUI-level abstraction does a backend implement, and what does it get for free vs. must reimplement?**

From the AGENTS.md, WaterUI's self-drawn backends (hydrolysis, dew) "share waterui-core, reactivity, layout, and text, and diverge only in their render/flush strategy." And there's a `ViewRenderer` trait (core/src/ui/view_renderer.rs). The native backends (apple/android/gtk) consume the view tree via the FFI (view_id/body/force_as_*). So there are actually TWO backend integration styles in WaterUI:

A. **Native FFI backends** (apple, android): consume the C ABI, traverse the tree with `waterui_view_id`/`waterui_view_body`/`waterui_force_as_*`, and subscribe to reactivity via `waterui_watch_binding_*`. They map to platform widgets.

B. **Self-drawn backends** (hydrolysis, dew): share core reactivity/layout/text, implement a renderer trait (ViewRenderer/GpuRenderer/SubView/Layout), draw themselves.

The Pathland backend is more like (A) in spirit — it needs to walk the tree and translate each view into opcodes — but it also needs reactivity wiring to emit SET_TEXT/SET_PROPERTY on signal changes.

Now the crucial technical point about how the opcode stream gets produced:

Pathland opcodes are **delta commands**: TREE (create_node, delete_node, insert_child, remove_child, move_child), STYLE (set_property, set_text), META (reset). To emit them, something must walk the WaterUI view tree and assign node IDs and emit create/insert opcodes, and then, when a Binding/Computed changes, emit a set_property/set_text for just the affected node.

Since the user explicitly does NOT want Pathland's diff/view/dsl/signal, the responsibility for change-detection falls on the WaterUI side. WaterUI has exactly the right primitives for this:

- **Initial tree emission**: walk the body() tree once, assign Pathland node IDs, emit create_node + insert_child (TREE), emit initial properties (STYLE set_property/set_text). This is the WaterUI backend's "render" of each raw view.
- **Property/text updates**: WaterUI's fine-grained reactivity (Binding/Computed watch) maps perfectly onto set_property/set_text. When a Computed a view holds changes, WaterUI's watcher fires → the backend emits set_text/set_property for that node. No diff needed — this is precise per-signal emission, which is EXACTLY what WaterUI already does natively (waterui_watch_binding_*). So "no diff from Pathland" is fine because WaterUI's reactivity IS the change source.
- **Structural changes**: WaterUI's ForEach/List already id-diffs membership (insert/remove/move by id). when()/watch() cause structural swaps. These map to TREE create/delete/insert/remove/move. Again WaterUI already knows the structural deltas (ForEach diffs by id), so no Pathland diff needed.

So the honest, precise answer is:

**Yes** — and it's a clean fit precisely because you're NOT taking Pathland's diff/signal/view. WaterUI already owns change-detection (fine-grained signals + ForEach id-diffing); it just needs a backend that *serializes* its view tree + updates as Pathland's 16-byte opcode stream. You'd author in WaterUI and get:
- Pathland's wire format + zero-copy ring + arena
- Pathland's network batch transport (remote projection / SSR → browser)
- Any Pathland renderer as a downstream consumer (existing GTK renderer, future browser/embedded)
- WaterUI's full authoring surface (components, forms, nav, gestures, theme, CLI, preview, testing)

The tradeoffs / things that need deciding:

1. **Which WaterUI backend trait to implement.** Need to inspect whether there's a clean renderer trait (`ViewRenderer`) that a "serialize to opcodes" backend can implement, or whether it must go through the FFI surface. The self-drawn backends share layout — but a Pathland backend doesn't do layout (Pathland is declarative, native elements lay out). So the Pathland backend is more like the FFI/native path: traverse the view tree, translate to opcodes. This suggests either (a) a new in-process backend crate that depends on waterui-core and pathland-core directly (cleaner, no C ABI), or (b) a consumer of the existing FFI. (a) is simpler and avoids the FFI pull model.

2. **Node identity.** Pathland opcodes need a stable u32 node_id per node. WaterUI's `Id`/`Identifiable` (core/src/foundation/id.rs) already assigns stable Ids — so you map WaterUI's `Id` → Pathland node_id. But WaterUI's Id is per-ForEach-item; the full tree needs per-view node IDs too. Need a scheme: assign node IDs as you walk body(). This is the main new code.

3. **Component/property ID catalog alignment.** Pathland's constants.rs has a fixed catalog (component_type HSTACK/VSTACK/TEXT/BUTTON/..., property_id SPACING/COLOR/FONT_SIZE/...). WaterUI has a much richer component set (form, navigation, media, video, charts, markdown, GPU surface). So you must extend Pathland's catalog (constants.rs + spec/OPCODE.md) to cover every WaterUI component/property you want to project, OR map a subset. This is the "catalog-driven" aspect — and it collides slightly with WaterUI's principle #2 (minimum FFI surface, compose in Rust). But since Pathland's protocol is the target, the catalog is the contract; you'd enumerate WaterUI's raw views in the catalog. This is real work and needs a decision about scope (which components first).

4. **Reactivity bridge.** Map WaterUI Binding/Computed (arbitrary T) → Pathland value types (F32/U32/Bool/Enum/Str). WaterUI's reactive values are richer (f64, String, Color, custom structs via Binding<T>). Pathland's wire carries a u32 value or arena string. So you need a value-mapping layer: numeric → u32/F32, string → arena, bool → u32, enum → u32, color → 0xAARRGGBB u32, etc. This is the "signal → opcode" bridge, but using WaterUI's watch mechanism, not Pathland's signal.rs.

5. **What "benefit from the rest" actually delivers.** The headliner benefit is: **remote projection + protocol conformance + a language-agnostic renderer target**, on top of WaterUI's authoring/CLI/preview/testing. The non-benefit: you do NOT get a *native* backend (Pathland is a portable/self-drawn realization in WaterUI's taxonomy), and you don't get WaterUI's existing native widgets — you get whatever Pathland renderer you point at.

6. **The "transport seam" is already designed for this.** `pathland_core::Frame` is explicitly documented as "the transport seam" — `Frame::from_parts(slots, arena, start, end)` lets any backend produce Frame views over its own buffers, and both the shared-memory `Host` and `BatchDecoder` produce Frame views. So a WaterUI backend can write opcodes via `Guest` (or directly into a buffer) and the same downstream Pathland renderer consumes it identically over shared-memory or network batch. This is a genuinely nice fit.

Now, is there anything that would make it NOT work / a strong caveat? Let me think about WaterUI's philosophy constraints:

- Principle #4: "bridge native first, then provide cross-platform self-drawn realization." Pathland would be a self-drawn/portable realization — fine, it's a deliberate backend.
- Principle #3: Pathland isn't "native" (it's a portable protocol), so it'd be classified alongside hydrolysis/dew as non-native. Fine.
- The fine-grained reactivity principle (#8): Pathland's opcode model (delta commands, only changes emitted) is actually deeply aligned with fine-grained reactivity — arguably more aligned than WaterUI's FFI watcher model, since it's "emit only the changed node's property". So no conflict there. Good.
- Principle #2 (minimum FFI surface): the Pathland catalog must enumerate raw views, which is a tension but it's a *protocol* contract, not FFI. The catalog is the wire contract.

So overall: it's feasible and clean. The main work items and the decisions to nail down are what I should present as a plan, and ask 2-3 clarifying questions.

Actually, I need to reconsider what "backend" precisely means in WaterUI's codebase and what trait it implements, because that determines the plan's shape. Let me quickly check whether there's a `ViewRenderer` trait and how hydrolysis/dew integrate. But WaterUI is a separate repo I only have via webfetch. I could fetch the relevant files. But maybe that's overkill for a plan; the user asked a "could I" question and I've already got a very solid answer. However, to make the plan concrete and credible, I should confirm:

- Is there a backend/renderer trait (`ViewRenderer`) that a non-FFI backend implements in-process?
- Does WaterUI expose the view tree in-process (Rust types) or only via FFI?

From the AGENTS.md I already know: `core/src/ui/view_renderer.rs` is "the canonical example" of the object-safe shim pattern with `ViewRenderer` + `AnyView`. And hydrolysis/dew are in-process Rust crates sharing core. So there IS an in-process renderer abstraction. Let me quickly fetch the core/src/ui structure and view_renderer.rs to ground the plan.

Actually, let me not over-fetch. I have enough to answer the conceptual question well and produce a plan with clear decision points. But grounding in the actual WaterUI renderer trait would make the plan concrete. Let me do one targeted fetch of the core/src/ui directory listing and view_renderer.rs to know the trait shape. This is worth it for a credible plan.

214: /// `eventReadCursor`. Same 16-byte slot layout as the guest → host ring.
215: #[inline]
216: pub(crate) fn push_event(
217:     event_slots: &mut [u8],
218:     header: &mut [u8],
219:     mask: usize,
220:     op: &Opcode,
221: ) -> Result<(), RingError> {
222:     let write = cursor(header, memory::OFF_EVENT_WRITE_CURSOR, mask);
223:     let next = (write + 1) & mask;
224:     if next == cursor(header, memory::OFF_EVENT_READ_CURSOR, mask) {
225:         return Err(RingError::Full);
226:     }
227:     let bytes = op.to_bytes();
228:     let off = write * Opcode::SIZE;
229:     event_slots[off..off + Opcode::SIZE].copy_from_slice(&bytes);
230:     header::set_u32(header, memory::OFF_EVENT_WRITE_CURSOR, next as u32);

243:     let write = cursor(header, memory::OFF_EVENT_WRITE_CURSOR, mask);
244:     // The POC host never lets the event ring wrap past the reader; drain only a
245:     // contiguous (unwrapped) run.
246:     if write < read {
247:         return Vec::new();
248:     }
249:     let count = write - read;
250:     let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(count);
251:     for i in 0..count {
252:         let slot = (read + i) & mask;
253:         let off = slot * Opcode::SIZE;
254:         let bytes: [u8; Opcode::SIZE] =
255:             event_slots[off..off + Opcode::SIZE].try_into().unwrap();
256:         out.push(Opcode::from_bytes(&bytes));
257:     }
258:     header::set_u32(header, memory::OFF_EVENT_READ_CURSOR, write as u32);
259:     out
260: }

16: /// consumers are granted short-lived `Guest`/`Host` views over the same buffer
17: /// via the borrowed methods, so opcodes flow in place with no copies.
18: #[derive(Debug)]

The two ring files serve different layers. Let me explain clearly.

`pathland-core/src/ring.rs` — the low-level ring primitive: operates directly on the raw byte slices + header cursors (`writeCursor`/`readCursor`). It has the `push()` function (the actual SPSC ring mechanics) plus typed `push_*` helpers (`push_create_node`, `push_set_property`, etc.) and the event ring functions (`push_event`, `read_events`). It's `pub(crate)`, no_std, knows nothing about "transport" as a concept — it just manipulates the ring slots in linear memory.

`pathland-core-transport/src/ring.rs` — the high-level `RingTransport` struct that *owns* the linear-memory `Vec<u8>` and `MemoryLayout`, and exposes the transport-trait API (`FrameSource`, `DriverTransport`, `InputSink`). It hands out short-lived `Guest`/`Host` views via `producer()`, implements `next_frame()` (FrameSource) and `send_input()` (DriverTransport), and `drain_events()`. Now I have a comprehensive understanding. Let me synthesize the plan for "preparing Pathland for creating a WaterUI backend."

The user's stated position:
- They want to prepare Pathland (the repo I'm in) so that WaterUI can consume it as a backend.
- Signals (and by extension node/engine/diff) are NOT applicable because WaterUI owns change detection.

So the goal of "preparing Pathland" is to cleanly separate the protocol/transport layer (which WaterUI will reuse) from the smart-application layer (view/dsl/signal/diff/node/engine), so a WaterUI backend can depend on a minimal, protocol-only crate.

Key findings from my research:

1. `pathland-core` currently bundles BOTH halves in one crate:
   - Protocol half: `opcode.rs`, `constants.rs`, `memory.rs`, `ring.rs`, `arena.rs`, `events.rs`, + `Guest`/`Host`/`Frame`/`SharedHeader`/`init_memory` in `lib.rs`.
   - App/emitter half: `engine.rs` (diff emitter), `node.rs` (retained tree), `signal.rs` (reactive signals).
   
2. The public API (`Guest`/`Host`/`Frame`) is ALREADY decoupled from `Engine` — `Guest` just calls `ring_fn::push_*`. So a WaterUI backend could use `pathland-core` today and simply ignore `Engine`/`Node`/`SignalStore`. But those modules still compile (cheap, no deps), and they're still re-exported unconditionally.

3. The transport crate `pathland-core-transport` depends on `pathland-core` but only uses the protocol surface (`init_memory`, `Guest`, `Host`, `MemoryLayout`, `Event`). So it's fine either way.

So the "prepare" work is really about *crate/feature structure* so WaterUI gets a clean, minimal dependency and a clear contract. There are a few options:

Option A: Feature-gate the emitter layer in `pathland-core`.
- Add `#[cfg(feature = "engine")]` (or similar) around `engine.rs`, `node.rs`, `signal.rs` modules and their re-exports.
- Default features = `["engine"]` so existing consumers (pathland-view, pathland-view-native, demos) are unaffected.
- WaterUI backend uses `pathland-core = { default-features = false }` → only protocol surface.
- Pros: minimal change, single crate, no new crate plumbing.
- Cons: `node.rs` is referenced by `lib.rs`? No — lib.rs re-exports `node::*`, `engine::*`, `signal::*`. With feature gating, those re-exports are `#[cfg]`-gated. The `Guest`/`Host`/`Frame` don't depend on engine/node/signal. So it's clean. But `engine.rs` uses `Guest` (crate::Guest), so engine depends on the protocol half, not vice versa. Good — one-way dependency.

Option B: Extract a `pathland-opcode` (or `pathland-protocol`) crate containing the protocol half, and make `pathland-core` (emitter) depend on it.
- New crate: `pathland-protocol` = opcode, constants, memory, ring, arena, events, Guest/Host/Frame/SharedHeader/init_memory, conformance.
- `pathland-core` = engine, node, signal (depends on `pathland-protocol`).
- `pathland-core-transport` depends on `pathland-protocol` only.
- WaterUI backend depends on `pathland-protocol` + `pathland-core-transport`.
- Pros: cleanest separation, WaterUI never even sees the emitter types. Matches the "transport seam" philosophy already in the code.
- Cons: bigger refactor, crate rename churn (pathland-view, pathland-view-native, pathland-render-gtk, demos, codegen all need updated imports), and renames could ripple into the Java/ffi. Also `pathland-core` name becomes misleading (it'd be the emitter, not "core").

Option C: Leave structure as-is; just document that the WaterUI backend depends on pathland-core and uses only Guest/Host/Frame/transport. Minimal/zero code change in Pathland.

The user said "I want to prepare pathland for creating a backend for waterui." This implies they DO want to do some preparation work. So Option C (do nothing) probably isn't what they want, though I should present it as the baseline.

Also there's a subtlety about the catalog: WaterUI's component/property surface is richer than Pathland's `constants.rs` catalog. For the WaterUI backend to project WaterUI's full component set, the Pathland catalog must be extended (or the WaterUI backend maps to a subset). This is a *protocol evolution* question (new component types / property ids, which per AGENTS.md requires updating spec/OPCODE.md + conformance vectors). This is a separate but important part of "preparing."

Actually, wait — let me reconsider what "prepare Pathland" most usefully means. The user is preparing the Pathland side so that the WaterUI backend (which lives in WaterUI's repo) can be built against it. The concrete deliverables on the Pathland side:

1. **Make the protocol half a clean, minimal dependency surface** (feature-gate or split crate). This is the main "preparation."
2. **Expose the producer surface clearly** — the WaterUI backend will use `Guest` (create_node/insert_child/set_property/set_text/reset), `Host`/`Frame` for a Pathland renderer consumer, `RingTransport`/`BatchEncoder`/`Batcher` for transport, and `Event`/`send_event`/`drain_events` for input round-trip. Verify these are all public and usable from an external crate. They are (Guest/Host/Frame are `pub`, transport traits are `pub`).
3. **Catalog: decide the component/property mapping.** This is the design question. Either:
   - (a) WaterUI backend maps WaterUI components onto the existing Pathland catalog (subset; e.g., vstack/hstack/text/button/spacer/scrollview/list/grid + style props). Native-feeling but loses WaterUI-specific components.
   - (b) Extend the Pathland catalog to cover WaterUI's full component set (form, navigation, media, etc.) — requires spec + conformance + constants + every renderer update. Big.
   - This is a decision the user should make; I should surface it as a question/decision point, not assume.

4. **Value-type mapping** — WaterUI's `Binding<T>`/`Computed<T>` → Pathland value_type (F32/U32/Bool/Enum/Str + arena). This is mostly a WaterUI-side concern, but the Pathland side needs a clear value_type story (which already exists: value_type module + color 0xAARRGGBB + arena strings + design tokens).

5. **Maybe: an "emit-only" convenience API** for the producer that doesn't require the retained-tree types. But `Guest` already IS that. So no new API needed.

6. **Tests/conformance**: if we split or feature-gate, ensure `check-wasm.sh` still passes (no_std + wasm32 for pathland-core), and `cargo test` green.

Now, what's the MOST important thing to nail down before writing the plan? The crate-structure decision (feature-gate vs split vs nothing), and the catalog decision (subset vs extend). These are the two big forks.

Let me also double check: does `lib.rs` `Guest`/`Host`/`Frame`/`SharedHeader` depend on `node`/`engine`/`signal` at all? Looking at lib.rs: the `use` lines are `arena`, `memory::header`, `ring as ring_fn`, `constants`, `events`, `opcode`. It re-exports `engine`, `node`, `signal` but the Guest/Host/Frame implementation doesn't use them. `drain_events` uses `Event::try_from`. So yes, the protocol half is self-contained; engine/node/signal are additive.

One more consideration: `conformance.rs` in both crates — golden vectors. Does pathland-core's conformance.rs depend on engine/node/signal? It might generate golden vectors via the engine. Let me note I should check, but it's minor — conformance tests can be feature-gated with the engine if needed, or moved. Actually, the conformance vectors are a spec artifact; if we split, the protocol-level conformance (opcode encoding, event encode/decode, batch encode/decode) stays with the protocol crate, and the engine-level conformance (diff emission vectors) stays with the emitter crate. I should verify what's in conformance.rs.

Actually, I've done enough research to produce a solid plan with the right decision points. I shouldn't over-read. Let me check conformance.rs quickly to be thorough about the feature-gate/split implications, and also glance at the workspace check-wasm.sh and whether pathland-view-native depends on engine (it likely does, since it drives the engine). Actually pathland-view-native drives the engine via the builder/engine surface, so it depends on the emitter half. That's fine — it would keep using default features.

Let me quickly check conformance.rs in pathland-core to understand its coupling.

- Protocol surface: `Event`, `category`, `component_type`, `style`, `tree`, `Frame`, `Opcode`, `init_memory`, `Guest`, `MemoryLayout`, `Host`, `listener`, `property_id`, `value_type`, `APPEND`.
- Emitter surface only in TESTS: `Engine` (host.rs:171, lib.rs:530) and `Node`/`Component` via `root_node.properties` etc. (host.rs:204,258 reference `root_node.properties` — that's a `Node` from the test constructing the tree). So render-gtk's *production* code is protocol-only; its *tests* use the engine + retained tree to build test fixtures.

This is important: render-gtk tests use `Engine` + `pathland-view` (dev-dep) to author a tree and emit opcodes, then render. So if we remove the engine, these tests need to be rewritten to emit opcodes directly via `Guest` (which is trivial) OR removed (since render-gtk is being deleted anyway in the end goal).

Given the end goal (remove retained view + renderer, use WaterUI), the renderer and its tests will be deleted anyway. So we don't need to preserve render-gtk's engine-based tests long-term.

So the full plan crystalizes:

## End goal
Pathland = pure protocol + transport:
- `pathland-core` → protocol only (opcode, constants, memory, ring, arena, events, conformance, Guest/Host/Frame).
- `pathland-core-transport` → unchanged (depends on protocol-only core).
- Delete: `pathland-engine` (the moved emitter: node/engine/signal), `pathland-view`, `pathland-view-native`, `pathland-render-gtk`, `pathland-render-gtk-demo`, `pathland-codegen`, `lib/ui/components.yaml`, `lib/java/pathland-demo`.
- WaterUI (its own repo) adds a `backends/pathland` crate that depends on `pathland-core` + `pathland-core-transport` and produces/consumes opcodes.

## The split step (intermediate)
Since the user chose "split", the split is: move `engine.rs`/`node.rs`/`signal.rs` out of `pathland-core` into a new crate `pathland-engine` (which will later be deleted). `pathland-core` becomes pure protocol. `pathland-view` and `pathland-view-native` depend on `pathland-engine`.

1. Split now (protocol out or emitter out), keep things building.
2. Later delete the emitter/view/renderer.

OR maybe they want to just do it all now: split the protocol into its own crate, and delete the rest immediately.

I think the cleanest interpretation, given they said "Split" then "Existing [catalog]" then revealed the end goal, is:

The split IS the mechanism to reach the end goal. The direction of the split matters: we should split so that `pathland-core` becomes the protocol crate (surviving), and the emitter moves OUT to a crate that will be deleted. That way:
- `pathland-core` + `pathland-core-transport` are the permanent deliverable.
- `pathland-engine` (node/engine/signal) + `pathland-view` + `pathland-view-native` + `pathland-render-gtk` + demos + codegen + java are temporary, deleted once the WaterUI backend replaces them.

--- lib/rust/crates/pathland-engine/src/lib.rs	
+++ lib/rust/crates/pathland-engine/src/lib.rs	
@@ -0,0 +1,28 @@
+//! # pathland-engine
+//!
+//! The retained view tree (`Node`/`Component`) and the diff-based reactive
+//! emitter (`Engine`) that turns it into declarative `TREE`/`STYLE` opcodes,
+//! plus the reactive signals (`SignalStore`/`SignalId`/`SignalValue`) the
+//! engine records during emission.
+//!
+//! This crate is `no_std` + `alloc`. It depends on [`pathland_core`] for the
+//! wire types (`Opcode`, `Guest`, `RingError`) and protocol constants.
+//!
+//! This is the "smart application" half of Pathland; the protocol/transport
+//! half lives in `pathland-core` + `pathland-core-transport`.
+
+#![no_std]
+#![forbid(unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn)]
+
+#[cfg(test)]
+extern crate std;
+
+extern crate alloc;
+
+mod engine;
+mod node;
+mod signal;
+
+pub use engine::{EmitResult, Engine};
+pub use node::*;
+pub use signal::{Dep, SignalId, SignalStore, SignalValue};

/// Color-valued properties (COLOR, BACKGROUND_COLOR, …) are emitted with the

        | property_id::BORDER_COLOR => value_type::COLOR,

        _ => value_type::F32,

}
